query: Single-phase high-entropy alloys have difficulty achieving a satisfactory strength–ductility balance. Earlier work introduced the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with a uniform, fine lamellar structure to enable large-sized production and obtain good strength and plasticity, but its performance still falls short of industrial requirements. Its use in aircraft and spacecraft fasteners further requires stability under extreme temperature fluctuations, long-term mechanical loading, room-temperature creep, and corrosion, while relevant creep and corrosion studies remain limited by sample-size and experimental-environment constraints. Given these limitations and design requirements, what single intervention could improve the alloy’s practical performance? Present one hypothesis that specifies the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted improvement over the starting material, boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a feasible experiment whose outcome could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A controlled heat‐treatment designed to induce short‐range ordering (SRO) at the phase interfaces of the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA will improve its long-term creep and corrosion resistance while retaining an acceptable strength–ductility balance.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast eutectic AlCoCrFeNi2.1 with a fine lamellar dual-phase (fcc/B2) microstructure.
generation.intervention: Apply an optimized intermediate-temperature heat-treatment (with a specific temperature and duration) that promotes the formation of SRO at the interfaces between the fcc and B2 lamellae.
generation.conditions: The treatment must be performed under conditions that promote SRO without causing overaging or coarsening of the lamellar structure. Subsequent mechanical and corrosion evaluations should be conducted at both room temperature and up to at least 700°C to simulate service environments.
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced formation of short-range order at the phase boundaries within the lamellar microstructure.
generation.mechanism: Induced SRO is expected to reduce atomic diffusivity and provide an effective barrier to dislocation motion, thereby retarding creep deformation under long-term mechanical loading. In addition, a more ordered interfacial structure can stabilize passive films and reduce localized corrosive attack, improving overall corrosion resistance under extreme temperature fluctuations.
generation.predicted_outcome: The heat-treated alloy will exhibit lower room-temperature creep rates and enhanced corrosion resistance under prolonged exposure, while the balanced high strength and ductility (compared to the as-cast state) are maintained or only marginally reduced.
generation.baseline: The performance of the as-cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA, which, despite its high fracture strength and ductility, shows limitations in long-term creep resistance and corrosion behavior under extreme environments.
generation.boundary: The intervention is expected to be effective only if the heat-treatment parameters are carefully optimized to induce SRO without degrading the dual-phase lamellar structure. The improvement should be demonstrable up to service temperatures around 700°C and under sustained mechanical loading in corrosive environments. Excess treatment leading to coarsening or undesirable phase transformations would negate the benefits.
generation.uncertainty: The precise degree of SRO development and its quantitative impact on creep and corrosion performance remain uncertain and will require systematic investigation. There is also a risk that the heat-treatment could adversely affect ductility if not properly optimized.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of AlCoCrFeNi2.1 samples: one set in the as-cast state and a second set subjected to the tailored heat-treatment aimed at inducing SRO. Characterize both sets using atom probe tomography (APT) to quantify SRO levels. Then, conduct standardized room-temperature creep tests and electrochemical corrosion tests (e.g., potentiodynamic polarization) at room and elevated temperatures (up to 700°C).
measurements: Creep rate (strain rate under constant load)
Corrosion rate (electrochemical measurements such as corrosion current density)
Microstructural analysis (SEM/TEM) to check for phase coarsening or degradation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the heat-treated samples do not exhibit a statistically significant improvement (for example, at least a 10% reduction in creep rate and measurable enhancement in corrosion resistance) compared to the as-cast samples—or if the targeted SRO is not clearly observed—the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Medium- and high-entropy alloys are an emerging class of materials that can exhibit outstanding combinations of strength and ductility for engineering applications. Computational simulations have suggested the presence of short-range order (SRO) in these alloys, and recent experimental evidence is also beginning to emerge. Unfortunately, the difficulty in quantifying the SRO under different heat treatment conditions has generated much debate on the atomic preferencing and implications of SRO on mechanical properties. Here we develop an approach to measure SRO using atom probe tomography. This method balances the limitations of atom probe tomography with the threshold values of SRO to map the regimes where the required atomistic neighbourhood information is preserved and where it is not. We demonstrate the method with a case study of the CoCrNi alloy and use this to monitor SRO changes induced by heat treatments. These species-specific SRO measurements enable the generation of computational simulations of atomic neighbourhood models that are equivalent to the experiment and can contribute to the further understanding and design of medium- and high-entropy alloys and other materials

High-entropy alloys (HEAs) can have either high strength or high ductility, and a simultaneous achievement of both still constitutes a tough challenge. The inferior castability and compositional segregation of HEAs are also obstacles for their technological applications. To tackle these problems, here we proposed a novel strategy to design HEAs using the eutectic alloy concept, i.e. to achieve a microstructure composed of alternating soft fcc and hard bcc phases. As a manifestation of this concept, an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 (atomic portion) eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was designed. The as-cast EHEA possessed a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure, and showed an unprecedented combination of high tensile ductility and high fracture strength at room temperature. The excellent mechanical properties could be kept up to 700°C. This new alloy design strategy can be readily adapted to large-scale industrial production of HEAs with simultaneous high fracture strength and high ductility.
